candidates.date_evidence: The opened article identifies itself as the special connect() issue 2014 and documents nameof.

candidates.reason: Objective-C already supplies selector construction and receiver capability checks that can support the emitted identifier and dynamic-target validation portions of a Swift interface.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: Selectors identify names across classes; receiver checks occur at runtime and neither operation resolves renamed Swift declarations.

raw_response:
Six existing mechanisms could contribute to this design:

1. **C# 6 nameof expressions** — https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/msdn-magazine/2014/special-issue/csharp-how-csharp-6-0-simplifies-clarifies-and-condenses-your-code
   Compile-time symbol lookup before emitting a member name provides a model for rejecting misspelled or missing method references written with their containing type. The emitted source name alone does not supply Objective-C selector mapping or overload selection. The opened article is dated to its 2014 issue.

2. **Objective-C @selector plus respondsToSelector:** — https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/Cocoa/Conceptual/ObjectiveC/Chapters/ocSelectors.html
   Selector construction and receiver capability checks supply an existing runtime representation and a validation option for dynamic targets. A selector remains shared across classes, capability checks happen at runtime, and renamed Swift methods still need a mapping. The archived chapter was updated 2013-04-23.

3. **Qt typed signal-slot connections** — https://woboq.com/blog/new-signals-slots-syntax-in-qt5.html
   Class-qualified member pointers and compiler checks demonstrate how callback registration can reject nonexistent members and incompatible signatures; lambda callbacks provide an alternative that avoids caller-written method names. This does not directly create an Objective-C SEL. I also verified public Qt implementation code through web-indexed GitHub results. The article's publication date was not established.

4. **.NET expression trees and MethodCallExpression** — https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.linq.expressions.methodcallexpression
   Representing a typed lambda as a method-call expression suggests extracting the chosen declaration from checked code and then consulting bridge metadata. Swift would need corresponding compiler support. Current API documentation was opened; a 2009 introductory article appeared in search results but returned 403 on opening, leaving historical verification incomplete.

5. **Foundation ExportAttribute selector metadata** — https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/foundation.exportattribute?view=net-ios-27.2-11.0
   Attaching an Objective-C spelling to a host-language method demonstrates preserving the foreign name at the declaration, where a checked reference could recover it. The attribute's string remains manually authored, so validation is still needed. The opened live documentation has unknown availability relative to the cutoff.

6. **GCC -Wundeclared-selector diagnostics** — https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-7.4.0/gcc/Objective-C-and-Objective-C_002b_002b-Dialect-Options.html
   Checking selector expressions against visible declarations demonstrates catching nonexistent selector names during compilation. This check does not prove membership in the intended class or translate imported Swift names. This is later evidence: GCC's release table dates version 7.4 to 2018-12-06; attempted older documentation retrieval failed.

These are candidate components and transfer mechanisms, not claims of deployment or demonstrated usefulness for this problem. The unauthenticated grep.app request was inaccessible, so code discovery used code-through-web fallback rather than successful native code search. Live and undated sources were not backdated. Prior model knowledge of Swift selector syntax cannot be erased and is recorded as a recognized-memory limitation.
